title: Kubernetes Deployments: desired state, ReplicaSets and rolling updates
subtitle: Read a Deployment manifest and predict the rollout and its failure modes. Concepts and manifests only: no cluster is used.

learner.topic: Kubernetes Deployments: how desired state, ReplicaSets and rolling updates work
goals: Predict what a Deployment controller does after a change to replicas or the Pod template
Explain why a rolling update stalls when new Pods never become ready
Choose readiness settings for a simple web service
learner.scope: Concepts and manifests only; no live cluster required

intake.capability: Read a Deployment manifest and predict the rollout and its failure modes

learner.startingKnowledge: Uses Docker and docker compose; has never operated Kubernetes

practice.realWorld: no cluster available; simulations and manifests only

decisions.decision: Offer the diagnostic so known prerequisites can get a quick pass; keep the full core route available.
Put an activity or practice before the explanation and include more in-app or real-world practice.
Guided and independent practice in every full lesson plus spaced review.
Size lessons to about 30 minutes and pack the schedule into sessions of that length.

assumptions: Documentation basis: kubernetes.io pages read on 2026-10-20. Their version menu lists v1.37 as the current documentation, and the pages mention features "since v1.37". The course targets the apps/v1 Deployment API as documented there. Not verified: that every page snapshot is exactly v1.37 (the pages themselves do not print a version number).
No cluster is used. Every activity is a labelled simulation or a static trace of a manifest, written by the course author from the documented rules. None of it is output from a real cluster.
Pod and manifest names (web, /healthz, port 8080, image tags) are illustrative course examples, not taken from the Kubernetes documentation.

Simplification: the Deployment controller interleaves scale-up and scale-down steps in ways this course shows as tidy rounds. The documented limits (maxSurge, maxUnavailable) are exact; the exact order of individual steps is not.

outcomes.text: Predict what the Deployment controller does (which ReplicaSet and how many Pods) after a change to replicas or to the Pod template
Explain, from maxSurge, maxUnavailable and Pod readiness, why a rolling update stalls when the new Pods never become ready
Choose readiness probe settings and rollout parameters for a simple web service and justify them

modules.title: Deployments and rollouts
modules.summary: From desired state to ReplicaSets, rolling updates and readiness

glossary.definition: What you declare in an object's spec, for example "3 replicas of this Pod template". Controllers keep working to make the actual (current) state match it.
A non-terminating loop that watches the state of the cluster and makes or requests changes to move the current state closer to the desired state.
The smallest unit Kubernetes schedules: one or more containers that share network and storage. A Deployment creates Pods from its Pod template.
The part of a Deployment (.spec.template) that describes the Pods to create: labels, containers, image, probes. Changing it is what triggers a rollout.
An object that keeps a given number of identical Pods running, using a selector, a replica count and a Pod template. A Deployment creates and manages ReplicaSets for you.
An object that declares the desired state of a set of Pods and manages ReplicaSets to reach it, replacing Pods gradually when the Pod template changes.
The replacement of Pods of an old Pod template by Pods of a new one. With the default RollingUpdate strategy it happens gradually, within the limits maxSurge and maxUnavailable.
The maximum number of Pods that can exist above the desired number during a rolling update. A number or a percentage; percentages are rounded up; default 25%.
The maximum number of desired Pods that may be unavailable during a rolling update. A number or a percentage; percentages are rounded down; default 25%.
A Pod is ready when its containers report ready; with a readiness probe, that means the probe is succeeding. Pods that are not ready receive no Service traffic.
A Pod is available when it has been ready for at least minReadySeconds (default 0, so ready means available).
A check the kubelet runs repeatedly against a container. While it fails, the Pod is marked not ready and is removed from the endpoints of matching Services.
How long the Deployment controller waits for a rollout to make progress before reporting it as failed to progress (default 600). It reports; it does not roll back.

routes.title: Core route
routes.description: Three lessons, then the capstone. About 90 minutes, in three 30-minute sessions.

intro:
You already run services with Docker and docker compose. Kubernetes adds a layer that keeps re-checking what you asked for and acting until reality matches it. In three short lessons you will learn to read a Deployment manifest and predict what happens when you change it, why an update sometimes stops half-way, and how a readiness probe decides whether it finishes.

How it works: each lesson starts by making you predict, then explains. Everything is a manifest or a labelled simulation. You need only a text editor; nothing here runs a real cluster, and what you see in the simulations is the course author's model of the documented rules, not cluster output. Documentation basis: kubernetes.io, read 2026-10-20 (its menu lists v1.37 as current).

diagnostic.intro: Two quick questions to set your pace. Nothing is hidden by your answers.

questions.prompt: You change replicas: 3 to replicas: 5 in a Deployment and apply it. What happens?
options: A new ReplicaSet is created and replaces the old one
The existing ReplicaSet is scaled to 5 Pods; no rollout happens
Nothing, until you delete the Pods
questions.explanation: Only a change to the Pod template triggers a rollout; scaling does not.

feedback.0: That is what a Pod template change does, not a replicas change.
feedback.2: The controller acts on its own; you do not need to delete Pods.

questions.prompt: In Docker you can see a container is "running". What extra question does Kubernetes ask before sending it traffic?
options: Whether the image is the latest one
Whether the container is ready, as reported by its readiness probe if one is defined
Whether it uses less than 1 CPU
questions.explanation: Running is not the same as ready. Services send traffic only to ready Pods.

feedback.0: Image tags are unrelated to traffic routing.
feedback.2: CPU use is not a readiness condition.

capstone.title: Review a rollout before it ships
capstone.task:
A teammate shows you this Deployment and says: "I'll change the image to v2 and apply it on Friday afternoon." The new image has a bug: its /healthz endpoint returns HTTP 500 for the first two minutes and then 200 only if the database is reachable (it is not, from the new network).

kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 4
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 120
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: example/web:v1
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
          periodSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 3

Write a short review (about 150 words) that: (1) predicts which ReplicaSets and how many Pods exist two minutes after apply, with the arithmetic; (2) states what the Deployment status will show and whether users are affected; (3) says what the controller will and will not do next; and (4) recommends one change to the manifest and explains the trade-off.

descriptors: Gives Pod counts but not from maxSurge/maxUnavailable
Surge = ceil(4 x 25%) = 1 and unavailable = floor(4 x 25%) = 1, so up to 5 Pods total and at least 3 available; derives the state of both ReplicaSets
Mentions failure but not the mechanism
Explains that unready Pods get no traffic, that old ready Pods keep serving, and that after 120 s the Progressing condition reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded
Says the rollout stops but not why
States that the controller reports but does not roll back, keeps retrying, and that a human must fix the template or roll back
A specific change (for example a readiness check that matches real readiness, or a longer deadline or a stricter surge setting) with the trade-off named

capstone.evaluation: Self-assess with the rubric, then compare with the model. If you have a colleague who knows Kubernetes, ask them to challenge your arithmetic. Optional, outside this course: reproduce the scenario on a disposable cluster of your own and compare. This course never ran one, so it cannot tell you what yours will print.
capstone.model:
Arithmetic. replicas = 4. maxSurge 25% of 4 = 1 (rounded up); maxUnavailable 25% of 4 = 1 (rounded down). So at most 5 Pods exist and at least 3 must be available. With one unavailable allowed, the controller can scale the old ReplicaSet to 3 and create 2 new Pods (total 5). If those new Pods are not ready, no more old Pods can be removed without dropping below 3 available. Expect: old ReplicaSet 3 ready, new ReplicaSet 2 not ready.

Status. Users are served by the 3 old ready Pods; the unready new Pods are removed from Service endpoints. The Deployment stays in progress until 120 s pass; then Progressing becomes False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded.

Controller. It reports lack of progress and keeps retrying; it does not roll back automatically. A human must fix the template or roll back.

Recommendation. For example, split the probe: make readiness check what this Pod needs to serve (and decide deliberately whether a database outage should make every Pod unready), and keep maxUnavailable low so a bad version cannot reduce capacity. Trade-off: stricter limits make rollouts slower; a probe that depends on the database can take every Pod out of service during a database blip.

Course decision: the capstone scenario is invented for teaching. The 3 and 2 Pod counts follow from the documented limits; the exact step order the controller takes may differ.
